hon. friend? I am not asking for a reduction of $97,000, but of $23,000 in this item No. 24, on page 9 of the civil government estimates.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am glad to
hear that it is not the larger amount, but what I have said would be equally applicable in that case; perhaps the force of my remarks might be increased. When my hon. friend asks that the civil government estimates for the Department of Labour be reduced by $23,000, I think it is fair to ask the committee to take into consideration the fact that the minister shows a reduction in
the main estimates for the Department of Labour, as presented to Parliament this year, of $100,000 on the amount asked for last year. I can readily see, that if hon. members wish to embarrass the minister, wish to make it difficult for a new minister requiring first knowledge of his department, and wishing to do justice to the members of his staff, they can probably make out a case from the estimates as brought down which would seem to show that some money asked for was hot required, but in view of what I have just said, and in view of the explanation the minister has made that some of the temporary clerks he is dispensing with altogether, were not paid out of corresponding appropriations to those he is referring to at the present time, and that the increase is accounted for by his seeking to disclose publicly to the House that he is making permanent a few clerks to take the place of a larger number of temporary clerks he has dispensed with, I hope my hon. friend from Centre Vancouver, under such circumstances, will not press his motion. If he should, I would ask the Committee to take what I think under the circumstances would be a reasonable attitude in considering the motion and bear in mind all that the minister has said by way of explanation, as well as his saving on the main estimates, and permit him at least the opportunity to get to know the work of his department before beginning to do an injustice to some members of the Civil Service who certainly will be adversely affected if a motion of the kind is passed.
Will the minister answer my question as to the amount expended under the item of $75,000 because that is important; that is what this whole argument is based on.

My hon. friend will understand that as the fiscal year expires to-night we could not accurately give him the information now. It might be of information to him, however, if I would state the results at the close of the last fiscal year.

Pardon me. I have asked my hon. friend for certain information. 1 am asking it in a conciliatory spirit and, having in mind the expressed wish of the Prime Minister that this motion be withdrawn, if he will tell me, or show me that a very substantial portion of the $75,000 has been expended on this the 31st day of March, or up to the 1st of March, it will go a long way to support the argu-

Supply-Labour
ment of the Prime Minister. If not I cannot see anything in the argument.

In answer to my hon. friend I would say that up to February 28th, 1922, $47,012.51 had been expended under Administration Employment Offices. I still would like to give my hon. friend some of the results that were before him at the close of the last financial year as indicating that he surely must have some knowledge of this situation. At the close of the last fiscal year we found that the civil government salaries $106,762.60 had been paid out, and that out of civil government contingencies $30,627.91 had been paid for temporary employees. For the salaries of Fair Wages Inspecrion Officers $12,269.84 had been paid; for salaries under the Conciliation and Labour Act $12,721.12; for salaries to Administration Employment Offices $50,953.93. I am sure my hon. friend will agree these are funds entirely different from those we are considering here.
That is the item referred to by the Prime Minister.

Temporary employees. Other items are: salaries joint industrial councils, $326.62; salary director of coal operations, $6,285; salary arrears under reclassification, $8,052.97, or a total for the last fiscal year of $228,139.34. That was as of March 31, one year ago to-day. Again, may I say to my hon. friend that last year the records indicate that the temporary employees in the Labour Department were paid from these sources: contingencies, 56; employment offices, 56; joint councils, 2. This indicates there were 114 temporary employees at one time or another, but there were only about 42 when I took charge of the department.

Do I
understand the minister to say that during the past fiscal year at different times there were 114 temporary employees employed in that department?
That is correct.
And do I understand the minister to say that the wages of these men were largely paid out of the vote referred to by the Prime Minister?
The figures were: employment offices, 56; contingencies, 56; joint councils, 2.

And on
the 1st January when the minister took

charge there were forty-two temporary employees?
Yes.
And the minister proposes to do away permanently with thirty out of these forty-two?
Yes, in so far as that may be possible.

And
twelve out of the forty-two are to be made permanent? Is that the situation?

In order that there will be no misunderstanding, let me say there is no provision being made in these civil government estimates for thirty of the employees I found in the Labour Department when I took office.
Then their salaries are not needed in the vote?

Unless it may be
necessary to utilize their services in some one of the branches,' and either pay them out of contingencies or some other of the various funds of the department as fixed by statute.

That does not affect
the fact upon which my motion rests. They are provided for in your main estimates of this year. I would say to my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) that the figure of 114 temporary employees given by the minister has no relation whatever, to the extent of forty-two, to the estimates under consideration now. The balance of them, and seventy odd employees, are provided for in item 272 to be found at page 52 of the Estimates. So we must not allow the idea to permeate the minds of hon. gentlemen that the number of temporary employees is being reduced from 114 to 12-that would not be correct at all.

I hesitate to ask a question for fear of eliciting another speech from the Minister of Labour. We have spent a great deal of time with these estimates and we have not made much progress. I would like to get information on a couple of points from the minister if he can answer me briefly. I understand that under the Civil Service Act the minister has no power to discharge any official but he can abolish an office. Am I correct in that understanding?

My understanding is that I could discharge an employee for cause, but I could not do away with the office.

Supply-Labour

Could you not do it
under Order in Council?

My hon. friend corrects me to the extent of saying that I could do so under an Order in Council, but no hon. member would expect me to abolish an office that was necessary and one in which there was work to be done.

I should think that perhaps you might dispense with unnecessary employees by degrees. For example if there were three clerks in an office it might be possible for you to get along with two. My next question is: To What extent have these estimates been increased by statutory increases to the clerks in the department?

The increase of
$23,400 in salaries is attributable to the statutory increases provided for in the Civil Service Act, and by the addition to the permanent staff of employees who have heretofore been temporary.
Is it not true that during the last fiscal year a number of employees of the department were working with the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, and were temporary on that account?
I am advised that a good many of them were blanketed in during the year, but I had nothing to do with that. It was done before I was there.
As a matter of fact, they were so employed.
I am told a considerable number were.
They were there for the express purpose of assisting returned soldiers in the department and were partially paid by your department.
No, I am told that none of them were for that purpose.

As I understand these estimates, the minister is taking 117 permanent employees to do the work for which he proposes to pay $195,000. The work which that 117 are supposed to do in the coming year was performed in the past year by 106 permanent employees, plus 42 temporary ones, and it cost the department $171,000 odd, plus the amount paid to the 42 temporary ones, taken care of in some other vote. Is that correct?
I think my hon. friend is substantially correct.
In that case this vote, so far from showing an increase, would, in my opinion, show a decrease, because 42 are provided for out of the difference.

No, 12. My hon. friend is in error. That is very ingenious, but it does not carry. My hon. friend has declared, and never denied, that he has given notice to 30 of the 42 employees, and1 that, as far as he and the Government are concerned, their salaries cease. He has included in this vote 12 additional ones, or 11, but he says that 12 temporary ones are transferred to the permanent list. The item is increased by $23,000 plus the contingencies. Twelve are paid out of $171,000 plus the contingencies last year.
No.

The salaries of the 117 employees which he is now asking for in the $171,000, plus the $35,000 contingencies. We say to the House this year, "Give his department exactly the same as you gave it last year, and do not give it $23,000 in addition." I agree that these twelve are included in the $195,000, but he has told us, with a spirit of reproach, that he does not intend to clutter up the department with temporary employees like his predecessor. That is a very commendable action. Then it is not under the contingencies, and. he can change the vote if he likes. It might have been better had I moved that the total amount be reduced and not specify anything. I specified the item for the purpose of clarity. Last year the Government paid for 117, just the same as they provide for this year, with $171,000, plus the contingency vote of $35,000. We are asked to do the same thing this year.
I would like to ask if the employees last year were not 106 plus 42 temporary, making 148 employees in the service.
At the close of the year.

Paid out of $171,000
plus-
I did not so understand it. I understood 106 of them were paid out of the $171,640 and the other 42 were paid out of some other vote.

Out of this $35,000.
Supply-Labour

The hon. gentleman from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) is entirely mistaken, Ibut it is impossible to explain, and I will certainly have to give up trying to explain. I am forcefully reminded of the old adage "There are none so blind as those who do not wish to see," and I am also reminded of the words of Kipling-
If you can make one heap of all your winnings, And risk it on one turn of pitch and toss,
And lose, and start again at your beginnings, And never breathe a word about your loss.
Poor losers are the cause of all this discussion during the last two or three days.

I had
hoped, by my remark, that I would help clear up this matter, but what is the use of trying to clear up this matter, if the minister proceeds to use it as an excuse to lecture his political opponents?

The motion of the hon. gentleman for Vancouver Centre is in effect for a reduction of some $23,000. He is moving to have the $195,000 odd in these Estimates reduced to some $171,000 odd. I take it that is impossible, unless he is going to force the minister to take away from the permanent staff of the Labour Department the twelve employees whom he has placed there. If the motion read that the whole Estimates be reduced by $23,000 I would see some sense in it. I do not think that motion can be properly dealt with in this Committee. It is something over which this Committee has no control. This increase for the year is mostly made up by statutory increases plus the salary of twelve permanent employees who are taken from the forty-two temporary employees. I do not think the motion of my hon. friend is in order at all, so far as the real gist of the motion is concerned.

I would like to get at the facts of the case, and see where we stand. Perhaps it is not our part to lecture political opponents or political friends, but I think a little less pugnacity on the part of the Minister of Labour would enable us to arrive at an understanding of the situation. I think, perhaps, we understand the situation regarding the permanent employees. There were 106 last year and there are to be 117 this year. I presume the statutory increases provided in the Civil Service Act cover that amount, making the average salary last year $1,619 and the average salary .this year $1,667. I suppose that is accounted for by the working out of

that machine which we have created, and for which we do not seem to have provided any brakes. However, that is a matter for discussion later on, but that is the way it has impressed us so far. We have made a machine we do not seem able to control. If there is a brake we have not been able to get our hand on it yet. The question seems to centre around a little question of fact: were those temporary employees last year paid out of that contingency fund of $35,000 or were they not?
Part of them were.

If they were paid out of some other vote, I can understand the position taken by the minister that it is necessary to have that amount for contingencies voted this year as well as the amount covering the permanent staff. It is simply a question of fact. If they were paid out of some other fund last year, then we need that amount this year. If the $35,000 contingency fund covered all the temporary employees last year, then I can see that there is something in the motion made by the hon. member for Centre Vancouver (Mr. Stevens). Can we get at this question of fact? Speaking for myself-and I think I may speak for those around me- I may say that we came here with a great desire to reduce expenditures. We do not want to handicap unduly a minister in getting acquainted with his department. When I began to look at these estimates, I was almost afraid to confess that I did not know anything about the matter; but since ministers are prepared to confess that, I do not know that we need be ashamed. We do not want to reduce any expenditure that is necessary; we do not want to take the position of "cheap guys," who wish to cut down the salary of a man who is really useful in his department because, after all, the man who is getting the low salary is not, by any means, always the poorest man in a department. Sometimes it pays and pays well to get good men, however much you have to pay them. That is our position. At the same time we want to impress upon this particular minister and upon the Government that it is our desire, if any means can be found of controlling this machine, to control it, so that we may not have this expenditure mounting up year after year without knowing when we are going to reach the maximum for civil government. Can we get at this little question of fact as regards the contingency fund, which may or may not

Supply-Labour
have provided for those temporary employees? If we can reach an agreement as to that point, we shall understand where we are.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The hon. gentleman's question of fact, which is a pertinent one, will I think, be answered by reference to the Auditor General's report. If hon. members will look at the Auditor General's report for the year ended March 31, 1921, which is the latest report published, they will find that a number of clerks received salaries paid from funds other than those represented in the appropriation that is being asked for at the present time. The same thing took place during the past year. The Auditor General's report for the past fiscal year, which ends to-day, cannot be presented to Parliament until next year; but it will show then that temporary clerks have been paid out of funds other than the contingency fund referred to here. It will be found that when the minister came into office fifty-six temporary clerks were paid out of the appropriation for employment offices, and as was pointed out this afternoon, the estimate for the employment offices has been reduced this year by several thousands of dollars. I do not think the hon. member for Centre Vancouver is anxious to embarrass us unduly. His purpose has been to make quite plain the difficulties that these Estimates involve and I think all the hon. members will realise that, seeking to follow what has been the custom of other years and to present the Estimates in a similar form, we have not been in a position to make the differences as apparent as we ourselves would like to have them appear. I hope my hon. friend's purpose has been served, and that he will not press his motion to a vote.

The Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock) stated clearly-and there is no doubt as to his statement, so far as I can gather during these two or three days' discussion-that the forty-two temporary employees came under this civil list; the fifty-six temporary employees to whom the Prime Minister refers, are provided for in another appropriation altogether on page 52 of the Estimates. My hon. friend is wrong in suggesting to the committee that we are seeking to reduce this vote by virtue of temporary employees being dismissed who were paid under another fund. Nothing of the kind. That point is the crux of the whole business.
The forty-two employees, of whom twelve are remaining, were paid last year out of the civil vote.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: If we were to discuss this for another week, we would not get very much further ahead, and if my hon. friend intends to press this matter to a vote, I hope he will let us take the vote before six o'clock.
The hon. member for Centre Vancouver should1 know that eighteen of those temporary employees are at present being paid out of the Employment Service appropriation.
Which is another vote altogether.
And two out of the vote for Joint Industrial Councils. That accounts for twenty of the forty-two who are not therefore, being paid out of any contingencies that are now before the committee.
Those two votes are in the other section of the Labour estimates.

Yes they are being
paid out of the Employment Service appropriation on page 52.
At six o'clock the Committee took recess.
After Recess
The Committee resumed at eight o'clock.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think it is desirable that hon. members should appreciate not only the difficulties which the present Government has, but the difficulties which the late government had, in the classification of the Estimates, and I would ask the indulgence of the House for a moment or two while I read a part of a debate which took place last session, and which will illustrate that the difficulties we on this side of the House are having at the present time in explaining our Estimates are precisely of the nature and character of those with which the late Government was faced when asking Parliament to pass its Estimates, and this as a consequence of its own legislation in giving certain powers to the Civil Service Commission and being governed in the reorganization of the Civil Service under those powers. I have in my hand Hansard of March 15th, 1921, when the then Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Tolrnie) was putting through his estimates. Hon. members who were in
Supply-Labour

the House last session will agree that no more conciliatory minister could be found than the then Minister of Agriculture, and the following is an illustration of the difficulties which he met with in endeavouring to explain the organization of his department. At page 935 of Hansard the following appears:
Mr. Cannon. Am I to understand the minister to mean that the Civil Service Commission has the right to fix the wages that shall be received by the civil servants in the employ of the Government, without the head of the department having anything to say about the matter?
Mr. Tolmie: The salaries and the increases are fixed by the classification.
Mr. Cannon: Does the minister refer to the classification that was made by those American experts imported into Canada, or to some other classification?
Mr. Tolmie: The classification brought into force about a year ago.
Mr. Cannon: By whom?
Mr. Tolmie: By the Civil Service Commission.
Mr. Cannon: Last week the Minister of Trade and Commerce explained during a debate in this House that experts brought into the country by the Government and who were absolute strangers to the Civil Service had made certain changes in the classification of the civil servants. Am I to understand that the changes which appear in the item I refer to were made by the experts or by the Civil Service Commission itself?
Mr. Tolmie: I understand that these salaries were fixed at the time the classification was made, but what part the American experts played in the classification I could not say off-hand.
Mr. Cannon: What I want to know is who made the classification? The Civil Service Commission, the Minister, or the outside experts?
Mr. Tolmie:	It was certainly not the
minister, but the Civil Service Commission. Whether they had the assistance of these imported experts or not, I could not say.
Mr. Cannon: The minister states he is not responsible for the classification of these employees?
Mr. Tolmie: The minister had nothing to do with the fixing of these salaries.
Mr. Cannon: But before the classification was made was not the minister consulted by the Civil Service Commission or by the experts, because, after all, the people who can give proper information in regard to the employees of a department are the head, the deputy head, and the branch heads? Were they consulted, and if so, did they make reports written or verbal?
Mr. Tolmie: The classifiers had a staff of experts of their own, and also consulted the deputy head before the classification was approved.
Mr. Cannon: Am I to understand that the deputy head of the Department of Agriculture is responsible for the classification of these particular employees? If so, I would like the minister, who is the head of the deputy head, to tell us the reasons for these varying increases.

Mr. Tolmie: The evidence of the deputy minister was taken by the commission, who came to their own decision.
Mr. Cannon: I should like to know from the minister, now that his deputy is here and can give him the required information, why the junior translator is getting a bigger increase than the translator himself?
Mr. Tolmie: Although the evidence of the deputy minister was taken, the final decision was in the hands of the Civil Service Commission. Therefore, I do not hold the deputy minister responsible for these increases that appear here. As I have explained before, there is the old classification and the new. This particular class of junior translator begins at a salary of $1,200 under the old system, with annual increases of about $50 a year up to about $ 1,6OiO. Under the new classification the minimum salary of translator is fixed at $1,440, with annual increases of $60 up to the maximum.
I think Mr. Chairman, it will be apparent to hon. members that the late government experienced the same difficulty in accounting for their estimates as presented to Parliament as we on this side of the House are experiencing to-night. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock) has explained that in presenting his estimates he accepted the statement made to him by his deputy minister as to what was the proper classification of the different clerks in his department, and the appropriate increases they were to receive, and that the estimates as presented contained nothing in the way of new appointments other than the making permanent of a certain number of temporary clerks.
I took advantage of the recess to discuss with the minister, with his deputy and others of the staff who had to do with the preparation of the estimates, the figures as they are presented. I find that the position is exactly as stated by the minister : that some of the temporary clerks have been made permanent. But there is this feature which has not been brought out, and which should be explained. If a deputy minister thinks that certain of his clerks ought to be promoted under the methods employed, the Civil Service Commission require that Parliament in the first instance vote the money for the position to which the advancement is to be made. After the money has been voted, the deputy minister has to go to the commission and ask its members to make the promotion. The commission may or may not carry out the wish of the deputy in that regard. The consequence of this method of procedure is that, in bringing down his estimates, the minister is obliged to ask Parliament to vote the money needed for the new position and also to vote the salary of the clerk in his

Supply-Labour
existing position in case he should not be transferred to the new one. In these estimates, six positions are cited which represent positions into which certain of the clerks may be promoted. Whether the Civil Service Commission will grant the promotions after they have been asked to do so, no one can say; until Parliament has voted the money and the promotion has actually been made, it cannot be a matter of certainty. The deputy minister states that these positions are provided for in the estimates in accordance with the requirements of the Civil Service Commission and the classification.
My hon. friend has a motion before the committee to reduce the estimates by a certain sum. I would like to make it clear that the acceptance of the motion will mean that the services of certain clerks in the department will have to be dispensed with, because there may not be an amount sufficient to pay the salaries of all the clerks whose positions are being provided for. The new fiscal year begins to-morrow; what we are asking Parliament to vote now is an amount necessary to meet these salaries during the coming year. I think the minister will find it possible to dispense with some of the clerks in his department; he intends to do so, in any event, when he gets an opportunity to effect reorganization. But the adoption of the motion may involve considerable embarrassment to some of the members of the service; it might make it necessary to dispense with the services of certain clerks a little more summarily, perhaps, than would otherwise be the case. I would appeal to the members of the committee to consider the Civil Service in this matter, and not to take a step which will involve no embarrassment to the Government but which may bring hardship on certain members of the Civil Service.

My hon. friend the minister, and, in a more moderate manner, the Prime Minister, read a lecture this afternoon to me and to others here instead of seeking, as the Prime Minister now has done, to give us an intelligent understanding of this matter. If the minister finds himself in a dilemma, it is his own fault. I asked him a very civil and pertinent question on Tuesday last; I got no answer to it. I asked the question a second time. I am not blaming him or even rebuking him for not answering my inquiry, but he got off on other topics. To-day I broached the matter again, and my answer was a lecture which, I may say, did not impress me very strongly. If a minister replies to questions by delivering curtain lectures, he is not likely to get very much consideration at the hands of those who are seeking the information. The Prime Minister and the Minister of Labour both sought to give the impression that I had no serious intention in pressing for the information I was requesting. Now, let me point out to the committee a few facts. The Prime Minister this afternoon very skilfully led the committee away from the point under discussion to another vote,-and I am quite sure, Mr. Chairman, had I been in that position you would have promptly called me to order-a vote on page 52, resolutions 268 and 272, dealing with the Labour Department proper. He conveyed to the committee information which was refused by the Minister of Labour,-who, indeed, gave us exactly the opposite impression-that the temporary employees involved in this discussion came under vote 272. Now, the minister gave us the impression very distinctly-and I shall not read long stories from last year's Hansard or this to support my argument-that he was reducing the large floating temporary staff, and he took upon himself great credit for doing so. I am in the judgment of the committee whether or not I reasonably interpreted the minister's attitude. He took credit to himself for that, and in his remarks he referred to this vote now before us. I came to the conclusion, as I think other members did, that he was reducing the staff which was included in the vote we were discussing; otherwise, why should he bring it in at all? If he wanted to take credit for reducing the staff by over thirty employees who came under another vote which we were not discussing, why did he bring the matter up? I submit I was perfectly correct in taking the minister's answer as it was given, although I am free to say that it was neither clear nor free from ambiguity. But I will meet the Prime Minister exactly on his own ground. He takes us over the votes 268 and 272, and I assume I shall be in order, Mr. Chairman, in referring to them; the Prime Minister transgressed the rules sufficiently to take us there.
I submit these facts to the committee in justification of the motion which I have presented: In votes 268 and 272 and the vote now before us we have three sums -I will give last year's figures first- $171,000 in vote 24; $75,000 in vote 268; $15,000 in vote 272, a total vote of $261,000. I asked the Prime Minister how much of vote 268 had been used, and after a great
Supply-Labour

deal of pressure we secured the information that up to the first of this month, $48,000 out of the $75,000 had been spent. I will add $12,000 more for this year, making' $60,000-and it will not amount to $60,000, I may tell hon. gentlemen. In other words that reduces the amount for last year to $246,000 in respect of the three votes-and the Prime Minister is weaving these supernumeraries into the three votes. The amounts for 1922-23 are as follows: $195,000 for vote 24; $45,000 for vote 268; $15,000 for vote 272, a total of $255,000. In other words, we have $246,000 last year as against $255,000 proposed this year. The minister has given us his solemn statement that to-night thirty employees cease to be employed by the department. He is asking for about $9,000 more for thirty employees less in these three votes,-and I care not how the Prime Minister juggles from one vote to another; the thirty employees are incorporated in these three votes.
Would my hon. friend tell us what figures he is adding, how he gets $246,000?

I went over that pretty well, but I shall not follow the example of the minister and refuse to give the information again. In 1921-22 the civil government vote corresponding with vote 24 this year was $171,000, in round figures; vote No. 268 was $75,000, and vote No. 271, $15,000. The Prime Minister tells us that those are the votes in which these employees are somewhere involved. The total is $261,000.
Where do you get $246,000?
I will give it to my hon. friend at once.
You said $246,000 just now.

Perhaps my hon. friend will allow me to finish the sentence I was about to utter. I asked the Prime Minister this afternoon how much of that $75,000 vote had been expended, and after a little pressure we got the answer, namely, $48,000; that applies to vote No. 268, and I say that I allow for this month, and it is an excessive allowance, an additianal $12,000, making $60,000 on that vote, or a total of $246,000. Now this is the point and the crux of the whole matter. That vote of $246,000 paid for the whole of these employees, both the ones included in the vote immediately under consideration

and the supernumerary group. Let us go a step further. The minister advises us that he is dropping thirty employees; I am clear about 'that.
My hon. friend has said so many times this afternoon what the Minister of Labour intended to do that perhaps I had better read the minister's language, so that there will be no misunderstanding.
I will read it.
It is on page 479 of Hansard.

On page 479 of Hansard a question was asked the minister and he replied as follows:
Mr. Murdock: The proposal is to make twelve of these forty-two temporary employees permanent. The other thirty have received notice, which so far as I understand will not be revoked, that they are to leave the service on the 31st of this month.
Now have I misstated the minister's language?
That is correct.

Then let me go back to my argument. For the sum of $246,000 a certain staff was maintained last year. This year there are thirty employees less whose services are to terminate to-night, the 31st of the month, yet the Government are asking $255,000 this year. I submit that there is no need to ask for $255,000 to provide for the services of thirty less employees when $246,000 proved sufficient for last year.
But that is not all. In the vote now before us the minister himself tells us that the position of Director of Technical Education, opposite which is the sum of $3,900 has been vacant for many months, I think nearly a year. He does not think it will be filled, but he is not certain. Then he states on page 479 of Hansard in regard to another individual, "I have no assurance that we shall fill this position." That was a position carrying a salary of $1,980 so here again there is an additional $5,800 for two positions which according to the minister's own statement there is no need to fill. So I submit to the House that in view of a reduction in the staff of thirty, and two other positions with salaries attaching to them amounting to $5,800 that the minister says he does not think will be filled, we are warranted in reducing this vote by $23,000.

Does my hon. friend take into consideration in that

Supply-Labour
computation he made by way of a comparison any statutory increases for this year? He is eliminating them altogether.

My hon. friend can
take what consolation he likes out of that interjection, but it is utterly void of reason and logic.
It is chock full of truth though. ,

Then I also say this: Last year, when these estimates were before the House, the then minister reduced them by $40,000. Why? I am not saying there was any particular merit in that, but the point is this: Exactly the same conditions apply this year as applied last year. During the war, and subsequently, there had been built up in this as in other departments extra staffs to deal with questions that were perhaps pertinent at the time but which to a large extent have now disappeared. Last year $40,000 of a reduction was made in these estimates, and I am informed that this year there should be a corresponding reduction in the requirements for this department. Indeed, Sir, when the Prime Minister himself spoke and carried us away from the vote under consideration to page 52 of the Estimates, he pointed out that the department had reduced the estimates on page 52. Now does not that reduction indicate that the activities of the department, and its main activities are covered by these main estimates, have been reduced by a corresponding amount? Otherwise, why the reduction in the estimates? If, therefore, there has been a reduction in the main estimates on page 52, does it not stand to reason that the head office expenses ought to be reduced accordingly? Is not that common sense?
The Prime Minister also made the statement that there were six duplications in these estimates. Let us pause for a moment to consider that. Why did not the minister tell us there were these duplications? He had his two deputies in front of him, and he told us that he required all of this. He said he might be able to weed some out, but the Prime Minister coolly tells us tonight that there are six duplications: that is, there are six clerks provided for here, and in order to meet some possible demand of the Civil Service Commission for possible elevation of officers to new positions, six new positions are provided. Does that sort of thing permeate the whole of these Estimates?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
In every department?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
It is a most extraordinary situation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It is.

What I suggest to my hon. friend is this: We have here a list of the votes in resolutions such as this: "Privy Council, $66,000." That is the resolution. Then details are given for our convenience, and the minister has a great many more details for his convenience, but the vote is a vote for a certain sum, and therefore I say to the committee we can very well afford to reduce the sum and then let the department work out these difficulties of duplications that have been mentioned. It is manifestly absurd for the minister to come before Parliament and ask us to vote sums on which we have no information at all. Let me put it this way to my hon. friends. If what the Prime Minister states is now the case, let us take these six duplications and segregate them so that they are not applicable to both votes. My hon. friend knows this perfectly well; supposing be elevates one of these clerks to a higher salaried position, he is immediately at liberty, by authority of Parliament, to refill the vacated position; he knows perfectly well that he is.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
My hon.
friend, I am sure, does not want to create a wrong impression. As I explained to him, that is part of the method of procedure adopted by the Civil Service Commission. They fill the new position. When they have done so, they take account of the fact that this money has been voted, not for the purpose of creating two positions, but for the purpose of enabling a clerk to be transferred at the appropriate time from one to the other. The minister cannot fill the position; his deputy asks the Civil Service Commission to give him a clerk to fill a particular position. The Civil Service Commission then takes account of the fact that when the Estimates were before Parliament one appropriation was put in to meet the possibility of this new appointment; that however, cancels the other-it does not create two new positions. This is simply a method of procedure which the Civil Service Commission has adopted to carry out what is necessary in effecting promotions.

I think perhaps it would be more correct to say that it was a method
Supply-Labour

discovered this afternoon, or this evening, by my hon. friend to explain this rather involved dilemma in which he finds himself.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No.

The bare facts are
there. A certain sum of money was required last year for a given service. This simple fact I place before the committee- and let me say to them that the same thing applies to other departments-the service is reduced by the number of thirty employees, and I say that we should not be asked to vote a larger sum by $23,000, than was required last year, for the payment of that reduced service. Now let me say this to the Prime Minister-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: May I ask my hon. friend this question: Suppose the Civil Service Commission should refuse to promote a certain clerk? If his salary is done away with what is going to be done with that clerk? From what source is he going to get his salary? The only way in which the payment can be provided in the meantime is for the estimate to be voted.

My hon. friend can vote his appropriation for the clerk if he desires. We are not objecting to that; we are objecting to this increase when there is a reduction of service. Just exactly how my hon. friend is to work it out is his business and not ours. Now let me draw the attention of the committee to another fact. I may be transgressing the rules 'but the Prime Minister has set an example in this regard. The Government claim-a statement was handed to the press in which they made the claim-a reduction of $138,000,000 in the general estimates of the country. The claim is made-we will not debate for the moment whether rightly or wrongly- that this is an economy effected in expenditure throughout the country. But if you take the Civil List you will find that in practically every department, with the exception, I think, of the Department of Railways, there is an increase at Ottawa. Now I bring this fact to the attention of the Government and I say: Personally I will co-operate with you in bringing about a reduction in the cost of administration in Ottawa because of the decreased service throughout the country. Now, if that is not logical I do not know what it is. Take any department; take the Department of Public Works, if you like. If there is a cessation of public works activities throughout 
the country surely there ought to be a corresponding reduction in the overhead cost of administration. Let me point this out to the committee: The very expedient employed by the late government, and condemned by the Minister of Labour this afternoon, is the method1 by which this can be brought about. And what is that? You will note that a year ago a reduction of $40,000 was made in the Labour Department. How? By dismissing or dispensing with the services of a number of temporary employees. We have been told by the Minister of Labour, by the Prime Minister and other speakers for'the Government, that you cannot rediuce the staff because they are permanent employees. The Minister of Labour says he cannot reduce the estimates because the salaries are for permanent employees. He is making twelve new permanent employees out of temporary employees this year. My hon. friend shakes his head. I do not know how on earth we are going to pin the Minister of Labour down to anything. He has told us time and time again that he is adding twelve temporary employees to the permanent staff. The committee knows perfectly well that what I am stating is perfectly true. Now what I am pointing out is this: The expedient of temporary employees is for exactly the 'situation that is facing us to-day. What is that? A reduction of the cost of administration throughout the country resulting from a cessation of activities due to the war and causes subsequent to the war. We can never get down from the war peak in the matter of expenditure unless we dismiss some one. Whom should we dismiss? Why the temporary employees certainly, and that is what the Minister of Labour of last year did. He reduced the estimates by $40,000; he laid off certain temporary employees. The present Minister has forty-two temporary employees and this number, when temporary employee's in other branches are included, is increased to 114. How can he reduce his estimates, how can he reduce his overhead, how can he reduce the cost of administration in Ottawa? Simply by dispensing with the services of some of these temporary employees instead of making them more permanent than they were. And so I say this to the Government: All through the main Estimates for the Civil Service in Ottawa there is a tendency towards a general increase; and I am not going to allow the Minister of Labour to get away with his curtain lecture to me this

Supply-Labour
afternoon, or the suggestion that I was aiming a blow at the working people in the Civil Service. I am doing nothing of the kind. I say to the Government that where they have efficient civil servants pay them a salary commensurate with their services every time; but it does not follow that the country must maintain a large staff beyond the needs and the requirements of the service. If the conditions to-day, as they were last year, are coming gradually back to normal, and we are getting away from the exigencies of war, then let us gradually bring the service down to a peace standard. Therefore what we say to the Prime Minister, and to every member of the Government, is that they will find us willing to join with them in a study of these Estimates for the one purpose of bringing about a reduction in the overhead charge, viz., the cost of administration in Ottawa.

Mr. Chairman, I sincerely regret if I have not been able to make the hon. member from Vancouver realize my viewpoint and my understanding in regard.to some of these things. I have tried several times to make it clear that, although in the estimates in certain cases perhaps there are two salaries, it is only intended to use one. Let me give a concrete case to illustrate my meaning, that of Mr. F. E. Harrison, Wage Investigator, Calgary. This gentleman has been for some time classified as a wage investigator at a salary of $2,340 a year. It has been contended-and here is the argument -that he should be named as a senior wage investigator beginning at $2,520 per year, a classification established by the Civil Service Commission. The vote in this particular case is to provide for the promotion of Mr. Harrison. In addition to his regular position he was formerly assistant to Mr. W. H. Armstrong, Director of Coai Operations, and was paid a salary of $600 per annum from War Appropriations for his extra services. While the position of Director of Coal Operations has been abolished, many of the duties pertaining to this position have descended to Mr. Harrison who performs them at a loss of $600 in salary. The department feels that Mr. Harrison should not suffer any loss, but as the limitations of the classification of his position and the regulations of the Civil Service Commission prevented the department from giving him the required increase in salary it was deemed advisable to create the new position of Senior Wage Investigator carrying a higher salary in
order that he might be permitted to receive the compensation to which the department feels he is entitled.
This is not an increase in the staff, but it proposes to establish two classifications with pay, only one of which will be used, under any circumstances, but if this $2,520 salary for Mr. Harrison's classification, as senior wage investigator, does not pass, we surely want to leave him with his present salary of $2,340, and classified as a wage investigator; otherwise we would have to come back to you and ask you to reconsider it. There is a number of exactly similar duplications in this proposal.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: By whom was Harrison appointed? That is important.
The Hon. Mr. Croth-ers, the late Minister of Labour, now deceased.
Is it not possible, if both votes pass, for the senior wage investigator and the other investigator, as proposed, for the Minister of Labour to appoint another man?

I am told that the
lower position would be at once abolished by the commission, when the senior wage investigator had ben appointed.
Why?
That is something I cannot answer.
Have you any wage investigator other than this man?
Yes.

Why should the
position be abolished?

I can only give my
hon. friend my word that the position will not be filled, and, furthermore, I will acquiesce in your view. If hon. gentlemen say that no more money should be paid for permanent salaries this year than last year, to-morrow morning I will proceed to put into effect the desire of this House, but not one temporary salary has been paid out of the vote of last year, or could be paid out of the vote of this year, and, therefore, any stress that has been placed on the forty-two temporary employees has no bearing upon this specific civil government vote.

As I understand the
minister, a larger salary has been put in
Supply-Labour

providing for the promotion of this investigator. He is not sure that this man is going to be promoted. If the position for which he is providing this salary is filled by the Civil Service Commission, we will have two employees on the pay-roll. Here is a wage investigator, as I understand it, at $2,300 a year. Then $2,500 is put in in the expectation that he will be promoted. If the Civil Service Commission say that he is not a suitable man, and they select somebody else, you will have two men on salary. Is that right? You do not lay off the wage investigator; you retain him in the position he occupies now, and you add another entire salary.
I am told we would at once drop the wage investigator.
You put in the man who now holds that position?
We would not accept any other man for promotion in place of this man, for whom a new official classification has been made.
Do I understand that in the promotion of this man, and the creation of a new office, the department has power to refuse the man selected by the Civil Service Commission?

The department would have the right to refuse to appoint any one. I desire the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken) to understand that this man is regarded as being specially entitled to some extra consideration on account of the special mining situation in District 18, and the fact that he has proven to be a valuable officer in British Columbia and Alberta. While war appropriations were being dealt with he was getting $600 more, but that cannot be paid any longer, and, therefore, the only way to give him a fair measure of justice is to make a slightly increased classification, giving him a couple of hundred dollars more than other investigators.
I am not objecting to his getting an increase or promotion, but I am stating that the Civil Service Commission is the body that will decide whether he is to be promoted or not. Am I right?

My hon. friend is hardly right, because they would not appoint without an application from us, and if they appointed anyone except this man, I am told the Labour Department would

not accept the appointment, and would not regard some other man as being specially entitled to $200 extra, and, therefore, the position would not be filled.
Then I do not understand the Civil Service Act.
Who does?

I thought the procedure was that the department notified the Civil Service Commission that there was a certain office to be filled. The commission then advertised for applications for the particular office, and held an examination, or an inquiry, into the man's capacity and filled the office. I do not object to this man being promoted, or getting more salary, but if the Civil Service Commission say "You having asked for a new officer, we do not think the man who was the former wage investigator is competent for it, and we will appoint someone else." Then I understand the appointment by the Civil Service Commission would stand. If they appointed someone else, then the department has not only the wage investigator on its payrolls, but also the new appointee. I do not see how you are going to get over that, unless the Department of Labour directs the course of the Civil Service Commission. If the minister tells me that he can control the commission that will explain the matter. I was under the impression that that commission was not controlled by the department. If it is controlled by the department, then patronage has not been abolished, and if it is not controlled, we are in danger of having two men to fill one job.

It came out pretty clearly last year, before the committee dealing with the Spinney Bill, that the deputy head of the department could make a recommendation to the Civil Service Commission, which was almost always accepted by the commission. I was a member of that committee and I think that was pretty clearly established.
Was that not with regard to promotions only?

Not necessarily. This would refer to a promotion, I understand. It was clearly understood in that investigation that the opinion, or the suggestion, of the deputy head would be accepted. I do not know that they are absolutely bound by that opinion, but it was established before that committee, certainly to my satisfaction that the commission accepted the recommendation of the deputy head. There-

Supply-Labour
fore, if the Minister of Labour or his deputy made his recommendation to the commission that this particular man be appointed,
I think there is very little doubt that the commission would accept that recommendation-at least they stated so at the investigation.

I wish to ask a question, and I am not asking it in a controversial way. It arose from a statement made by the Prime Minister, which struck me as being of considerable importance, and I should like to get a clear understanding of it. If I mistake not, it was said that, not only in this department, but in others, the necessity arose at times practically to duplicate positions in the Estimates in order to provide for possible or probable promotion from one position to another, and in order to allow for that, a salary was provided for each position, with the understanding that only one salary would be used.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is the case in some of the departments.

In that case, is it necessary to provide for both salaries? Would it not be sufficient, in cases like that, to provide for a salary to cover the higher position of the two, because the greater always contains the less, and in case the promotion was not made, the salary appropriated for the higher position would still pay the salary of the lower position.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
My hon.
friend is quite right. I am informed that, in some departments, what he has suggested is done, but in others, the other course has been adopted.

That is the way I have understood the act to be worked out; but does that not all go to show that this motion should pass? The motion is made on the ground that there is not so much to provide for this year as last; that is to say, that the Labour Department, in the scale of its operations, would be smaller rather than larger, on account of the assurance of the minister that the number of employees would be less, as undoubtedly they should be less? The number has been growing progressively less for some time. Objection is taken on this ground

this is given as an illustration of the objection-that it is necessary to name in the Estimates two positions to cover the event of the man who fills what is now only the one position, the lower, not being chosen by the commission to fill the higher. The minister says: "Well, if he is not chosen, we shall not accept the other choice." I think he is right in saying that the department has power to refuse the choice of the commission. In that case only one salary is going to be required, and if the higher one is provided for, undoubtedly that is all that is necessary. Supposing there is simply a general cut ordered by this committee. Then it is certainly within the power of the department to allocate that cut so that just the six duplications will absorb a good part of it. Consequently, there is no argument in the case of duplication against the cut being made.
Mr.MACKENZIE KING: I think my right hon. friend is quite correct so far as he goes. The sum which the hon. member for Centre Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) has proposed is an arbitrary and rather a large amount. Without opportunity for adjusting all these estimates very carefully, it is difficult to say just what amount could be saved. If my hon. friend from Vancouver would consider reducing his amount somewhat, possibly the hardship of which I have just spoken might be avoided; but to take the sum which he has suggested and deliberately pass it in this committee, I am afraid, would create hardship upon some members of the Civil Service.

I should like to ask the minister whether with reference to two positions provided for in the estimates, a substantial saving might not be made. On page 107, the third position is that of Director of Technical Education. As I understand the matter, the legislation under which this office was created was passed in 1919, and Dr. Gill was appointed Director of Technical Education either in the latter part of 1919 or in the early months of 1920. In carrying out the provisions of the act, it was found that it was necessary for the Director of Technical Education to visit the different provinces for the purpose of making the necessary arrangements for the proper working of the act, and that required that the director should be absent from Ottawa a great part of his time. That was found to interfere with the carrying on of the office at Ottawa; and in order to carry on the negotiations with the provinces, later on an Assistant Director of Technical Education was appointed. We have a Director of Technical Education, and for the last year the appropriation was $4,275. This year the appropriation is $3,900. The arrange-

Supply-Labour

ments, as I understand the matter, have all been completed with the provinces, and on the first of September of last year, Dr. Gill resigned. Mr. Crawford was appointed Assistant Director of Technical Education, and from the first of September of last year until the 29th of December, when the late government went out, Mr. Crawford was carrying on, performing the duties of Director of Technical Education. It was the intention of the late government that no appointment would be made to fill the vacancy; that Mr. Crawford should be promoted to be Director of Technical Education. It was found that the reason for the appointment of the assistant had passed.
All arrangements had been com-
9 p.m. pleted between the department at Ottawa and the provinces, and the Director of Technical Education was again in a position to carry on his work here. The late government was in office from the first of September until the 29th of December, and no appointment was made to fill the vacancy. Why? Simply because it was the policy of the government to do away with the assistant and to let the director again carry on at Ottawa. There is really no work outside of Ottawa, and it was the policy of the ex-Minister of Labour and of the late government that the Director of Technical Education should be a fountain of information only; that he should be in Ottawa for the purpose of giving to the provinces information that they might write for, so that these two offices are clearly not necessary, unless the present minister has changed the policy of his predecessor in office and has some other policy for the administration of this act. If he has, I am sure he will tell the House what that policy is. If he has no other policy, surely it is unnecessary to provide a salary of $3,900 for the Director of Technical Education and a salary of $3,705 for the assistant director. I do not know whether any appointment has been made since the 20th of December last or not; but I know that prior to that time no appointment had been made, and that the late government had no intention to make any appointment. There you have a clear saving of $3,705. With another item here, the two would make a saving of more than $5,000. I should like to know from the minister, in connection with the second item on page 108, "Confidential Messenger," who the confidential messenger was last year.
I am advised that Mr. Lacelle was confidential messenger last year and is this year, as proposed.
When was Mr. Lacelle appointed?
In 1906, I am told.
Was a Mr. Rump not confidential messenger last year?
I am advised that he was promoted to a clerkship, and that he earned his promotion by passing the specified examination. He has been there since I have been in office.

If I were to claim that when Mr. Rump was placed in another department no appointment to the office of confidential mesenger was made, that would not be according to what the minister understands to be the fact?
I am told that Mr. Lacelle has been a messenger since 1906, and that he was made confidential messenger some two or three years ago.
Did Mr. Lacelle occupy the position which in the estimates $1,200 was provided for last year?
The estimates as I have them before me so indicate.
That is your answer ?
Yes sir; and he did occupy the position to the best of my knowledge and belief.
Will the minister kindly explain the position of the department with reference to the appointment of a Director and Assistant Director of Technical Education?

Gladly. The position of Director of Technical Education was vacant when I assumed office. I understand that Dr. Gill, who ocupied the position, went to British Columbia at a substantially increased salary some time early in September last. My predecessor in office very kindly left me a memorandum in regard to Dr. Gill, and the hon. member for Lanark has explained fully to the House the recommendation and suggestion made to me at the time I took office. The position has not been filled yet, although numerous applications have come to me, and I have not thought of filling it at the moment. We have in the department an Assistant Director of Technical Education. With my knowledge of his abilities and of the work to be performed, I do not care at the present time to promote him to the director-

Supply-Labour
ship. I do not see the necessity of having two officers at present, but I do not know whether that condition will continue. It is only proper to say, though, that this year there are $1,000,000 to be handled under the direction of either the Director or the Assistant Director of Technical Education. I am told that each year agreements have to be made between the federal government's representative and the educational authorities of the provinces with regard to the expenditure of this fund, and that it requires a very capable officer to see that the appropriation is judiciously expended. That is as I understand the situation with regard to the Directorship of Technical Education. I think the hon. member will agree that it would not be advisable for me to strike out the position of director and leave in the position of assistant director-in other words, an assistant to a position which does not exist. Therefore, at present the two positions are left in, although one is vacant.

If it is intended to promote the Assistant Director of Technical Education to the position of Director, surely the position of Assistant at $3,705 should be struck out of the estimates; or if it is the intention to continue the assistant, then the position of director at $3,900 should be struck out. It is not intended to continue the two positions?

Would it be consistent to strike out the Director of Technical Education and leave in the Assistant Director? If my hon. friend, as a business man and member of this House, will advise that course, I will agree with him at once.
No. I would suggest to the hon. minister that he follow what I stated to have been the policy of the late government-promote Mr. Crawford.
I am not prepared to do that, Sir, at present.

But that
would not be any reason why both appropriations should be kept in the estimates.
Why not strike out the appropriation and leave the position there?

Mr. Chairman, the
Prime Minister made a very reasonable suggestion, and I want to bring it to the attention of the committee as early as possible. I would suggest that my resolution which now reads:
37J
That in view of the statement of the Minister of Labour as appearing on page 479 of Hansard that thirty employees of the department would be dismissed on this day, March 31, 1922, item 24 on page 9 of the Estimates be reduced to the same amount as last year, namely, $171,640 for salaries and $35,000 for contingencies.
Instead of that I would move to substitute therefore:
That item 24 on page 9 of the Estimates be reduced by the sum of $15,000.
This, I have calculated somewhat carefully, will pretty well cover these points upon which we are agreed there will be required no vote. If the Prime Minister is agreeable to that, I would amend my motion accordingly.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: If the House will agree, I think we shall save time by accepting the hon. gentleman's amendment.

Mr. Chairman, I have been waiting for an opportunity to address the committee briefly. I am delighted with the zeal for economy shown by my hon. friends to my right. They have made a great deal of progress during the past year in the right direction, and I hope that that progress will continue. It did seem to me that my hon. friend from Lanark (Mr. Stewart) was on pretty good ground with respect to this Directorship of Technical Education. I expressed my opinion yesterday on that question, and 1 need only make this further observation now, that the position of Assistant Director of Technical Education might very well be dispensed with. If the minister does not wish to promote the present occupant of that position to the senior position, he might leave him in an active capacity in the other, at any rate, until he had made up his mind whether or not he wished to make that promotion. In fact, I am pretty well convinced that there is no need for either, and I think that the deputy minister or the minister himself, might very well be able to make the necessary arrangements with the provincial authorities covering the expenditure of this money, which in my judgment should never have been voted to the provinces for this purpose. But let that pass.
There is one other aspect of these estimates that I wish to briefly bring to the attention of the minister, and I do it not in any spirit of captious criticism, but with a real desire to assist him. I observe there are several items in the estimates for statistical clerks. Altogether we are providing about $27,000 for twenty-two stat-
Supply-Labour

istical clerks in the Department of Labour. We have a Bureau of Statistics, a branch of the Government service which in my judgment is very efficiently manned and operated. Would it not be possible for the Department of Labour to have its statistical work done, in large measure at least, in the Bureau of Statistics? The offices of the Labour Department are only a few blocks from those of the Bureau of Statistics; the bureau has all the machinery and equipment necessary to carry on the work. Are we to understand that the Department of Labour are building up within their own confines another statistical bureau? I mention this because I know how easy it is to duplicate services in government departments in this city. Another question I would ask is whether the Department of Labour is being equipped with the machines that go with statistical research work and which are already installed in the Bureau of Statistics?

At present we are
merely continuing the plan which, as I understand, has been in effect for very many years. These statistics collected in the Department of Labour are in connection with employment questions, the cost of living, and other matters coming within the purview of the department. I may tell my hon. friend, however, that for the past couple of weeks two or three ministers who think there is unnecessary duplication of statistical work have had it in mind to confer with the deputies of the respective departments and their chief officers with a view to finding out where those duplications can be eliminated, and how the collection of statistics can best be made uniform and placed under the supervision of one department only. I could place before you correspondence indicating that that matter is now under advisement and awaiting the time when we shall be able to get together for that purpose.

I am delighted to hear
that statement from the minister. I am very certain that if the committee of the Cabinet prosecute their inquiries diligently, as I am sure they will, very considerable saving can be effected. I may not be fully conversant with the circumstances, but there appears to be no good reason why this information gathered from different parts of the country for statistical purposes cannot be turned over to and compiled by the Statistical Bureau, with a consequent saving of thousands of dollars to the other departments.
fMr. Crerar.]

I make no criticism at all of the vote; in fact, I am disposed to think it is necessary. But it is only right that the committee should know that the concentration of statistics has been the work mainly of the last two years. The statistics formerly were prepared in every department-Railway Department, Trade and Commerce, and all the rest, and the result was not duplication, but triplication and quadruplication and all the other "cations." They have, however, been concentrated in the Trade and Commerce Department, under a very efficient officer, Mr. Coats, who stated in a recent address that, in his belief, we now had the best statistical service of any country in the world. That has been the work of late years. I do not rise particularly to emphasize that feature of the late administration, but possibly I can be justified in doing so in view of the taunt that has just been flung at us that our enthusiasm for economy is of recent birth.

Another thing that the
Government might well consider is the question of what statistics are really valuable, and what are not. As an illustration of statistics that are not very valuable I recall the case of a man in our community who used to bucksaw wood and who could tell you at the close of the day exactly how many sticks he had cut. He marked it down and kept a faithful record; in other words, he accumulated statistics. We had a very ponderous volume put into our hands since we came here, the Canadian Atlas, a magnificent volume, splendidly printed on paper of excellent quality. I turned over the pages the other day and I came across this heading: "Tons of freight per head of population." Now, that information is entombed in this ponderous volume. It reminds me of going into a museum and finding the mummies of cats and hawks and other vermin that were taken from the pyramids of Egypt. The Government might very well consider whether it is wise or necessary to publish statistics that are not of permanent value. One of the things that makes us speak as we do in regard to the reduction of expenditure is that the wheat crop of Manitoba is said not to be able to pay the taxes of this year.

Mr. Chairman, I did not intend to take part in this discussion, but as its range seems to have stretched from Dan to Beersheba and has proceeded, whether relevant to the item under consideration or not, I wish to suggest that

Supply-Labour
when the Government are co-ordinating, so to speak, the statistical branches of the various departments they consider seriously the advisability of eliminating at least fifty per cent of the civil servants employed in the inside service at Ottawa. I am an old civil servant; I had about four years' experience in the Department of Marine and Fisheries at Ottawa, and during that time I was forced to the conclusion that the service at Ottawa is overmanned, and, to great extent, overpaid. The people of my constituency are up in arms against the conditions prevailing in Ottawa with regard to the Civil Service. The late government gave us what was termed Civil Service improvement or Civil Service reform. A few, days ago I went over to the department in which I used to be employed, and I found that where there were two employees in 1914, in many of the branches to-day there are fifteen or sixteen, drawing pay from the public treasury. The farmers and the labouring men of Hants object to the public funds being dissipated in this manner. This afternoon we spent a great deal of time in the consideration of a matter involving $4,000 or $5,000; and we spent about $25,000 or $30,000 of the public moneys in useless discussion, largely owing to the fact that the ministry have inherited from the Government which was driven from power on the sixth of December a legacy for which the people owe them nothing but Christian forgiveness-to say the least. My only object in rising this afternoon is to ask the Administration, when they take into consideration the t co-ordination of the statistical branches, to give serious attention also to the reformation of the inside Civil Service-without going to the United States for assistance and without accepting the legacy which was handed down to us by the late administration.

I have much pleasure in endorsing the remarks of the last two speakers, although my experience has been from a different point of view. While it is highly desirable that we should save the money that is spent in handling and tabulating these returns when they are brought in, the people who excite my sympathies are the wretched people in the country who have to make them out. There are a large number of retailers in Canada -I forget the exact number-and it was a plank in my platform that I should endeavour to eliminate these useless returns. They are a perfect pest to the body of retailers throughout Canada. A
merchant in a big way in Vancouver told me they had to employ an extra clerk to make out the returns; this was more particularly during the war. Every time they sold a sack of potatoes all these different returns had to be made out, and not only did they have to keep an extra clerk for that work, but a very capable clerk, a statistician, indeed, to cope with it. I know one case where a storekeeper got one of these wretched returns and sat down and wrote on it,' "I will go to gaol before I will attempt to fill out this return." He simply could not do it and was not going to lie about it. This going- [DOT] to goal part of the business is no fantasy, because nearly all these returns have a notice at the bottom that if the return is [DOT]not sent in by such and such a date you are liable to so many days in gaol. The company I am associated with have had a number of returns to make out, and while we fibbed a little we generally got them out a month or so late, and mailed the things in. One in particular I had mailed, but it did not appear to have reached the department, because I got a registered letter to say that on account of its not being sent in I was liable to,
I forgot hoW many months in gaol, and they rather indicated they expected me to go to gaol by registered letter forthwith.
I had no way of proving that I had sent the return in, although I knew perfectly well I had sent it in. The company I am connected with also sells coal, and we have a monthly coal return to fill in. It is made out in such a way that no known system of book-keeping can be used in making out the return. We fake the thing as a matter of fact. Every sale is supposed to be tabulated in this miserable return, and we simply have to fill it out more or less by guess. And if that were not enough, about every three months, or to be quite safe, every six months, they change the whole system of making out the returns so they cannot be of any possible use to them for purposes of comparison. Hon. gentlemen are inclined to laugh, but it is a matter of deadly earnestness to a great many people. I am often at a loss to know and often wonder whether it will be myself or my book-keeper who will go to gaol eventually. Certainly one of us will. If the Government will eliminate some of these returns they will certainly earn the gratitude of the very large body of retailers throughout Canada.
Amendment (Mr. Stevens) agreed to: yeas 120, nays 0.
