Before the resolution as amended is agreed to I would like to ask if it is the intention of the Department of Labour to be represented at the Genoa Conference by a labour representative of this Dominion.

If my hon. friend is referring to the Conference in April, we shall be represented by Colonel Carnegie. I think the conference my hon. friend refers to is at Rome, not Genoa. The governing body of the International Labour Office meets at Rome in April.
I am speaking of the Economic Conference at Genoa.
We have nothing to do with it.	*
I think Canada is represented at the Genoa Conference by Sir Charles Gordon.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: And Professor Montpetit.
Is it the intention of the department or of the Government that labour shall be represented at that conference?
We have had no invitation to be represented at that conference.

The conference is for the consideration of economic and financial questions which are vital to the interests of Canada, questions in which labour as well as capital has a very deep interest. I should like to ask the minister if, in his opinion, in the consideration of these matters the interests of labour would be well taken care of by Sir Charles Gordon.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Perhaps I
might answer my hon. friend. An invitation was extended to the Government of Canada to be represented at the Genoa Conference. It was intimated that one or two delegates might be appointed, but the Government has chosen, as my hon. friend has mentioned, Sir Charles Gordon and Professor Montpetit. As my hon. friend is probably aware, Professor Montpetit is professor of economics in the University of Montreal and is well versed in labour and other problems. I am sure that in the hands of these two gentlemen the interests of labour, so far as they are matters for special concern, will be represented at this conference. It was not especially requisite that any particular group or class should be represented.

I do not
wish at all that my question should indicate that I have any fault to find with the selection made by the Government. If I were to express my own view I should say that in the selection of Sir Charles Gordon no happier or better choice could have been made for Canada. I simply desired to know whether in this conference, as in past international conferences, it was the intention that the Department of Labour, or labour, should be specially represented by a labour representative.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
May I point
out to my hon. friend that this conference is very similar in character to the conference at Washington. The late government when asked to appoint delegates to Washington selected Sir Robert Borden to represent this country; it was not thought advisable to appoint a special labour representative to that conference. The same reasons that governed the late administration in their appointment have also actuated the present Government.

May I tell my hon.
friend furthermore that I do not know of a better economist in Canada than Professor Montpetit and he is not more of a capitalist than myself. Besides I do not see why a labour man should be appointed at this conference any more than a farmer or a person engaged in any other trade or occupation in Canada.

I am entirely satisfied; I simply wished to get the position the Government took. _ There is another question I would like to ask the Minister of Labour before this matter is finally disposed of and that is: Is it the present policy of the minister to promote, or to attempt to promote, further good relations between employers and employees, particularly in the building trades? I find that in January last the minister is reported to have said that employers and employees in the building industry "must and shall get together." Now if my hon. friend is correctly reported I think it is possibly due to the committee that we should know what the policy of the Labour Department is, particularly in view of the fact that after that statement was reported by the press to have been made by the minister, the Fourth Annual Conference of the Association of Building and Construction Industries, held in the city of Hamilton from January 17th to 20th, passed this resolution :

Supply-Labour
Resolved, that in our industry we have found Joint Industrial Councils tend only to cause dissension rather than cure it, and therefore such councils should not be continued.
I would like to have the minister state to the committee whether in view of the fact that earlier in the month of January he is reported to have stated-if he was incorrectly reported of course that disposes of the matter-that the employers and the employees must and shall get together, the department has any policy for dealing with the situation in view of the resolution passed in Hamilton.

I am glad to advise
my hon. friend, although I am sure he is already aware of the fact, that the Labour Department has no authority to compel pleasant, proper and consistent relations in the building trades as between employer and employee. I can however, inform the hon. member that anything that can be done in a suggestive way will be done, any assistance that can be rendered will be rendered, in order to bring about, to create and to maintain proper- relations between employer and employees in the building trades. That is being done from time to . time. Occasionally we have suggestions as to how we can assist in that respect, and in every case we undertake to do whatever it appears possible to do to bring about, establish, and maintain the relations which should exist between employers and employees. But again I repeat my hon. friend is as familiar as I am, if not more so with the knowledge as to how far, under the existing federal regulations, the Labour Department can go in a matter of that kind.

It was only in view of the language used by the minister himself "must and shall" that I asked for information as to what the policy of the department was. Now I have one more question to ask and then I am through. In the Toronto Globe of November 24, 1921, the minister is reported to have expressed himself as follows:
I have been long-big- for two years to appear before a proper tribunal in order to get the facts as to the manner in which the rights of the people of this Dominion have been sacrificed and intentionally so. But no opportunity will come until after December 6th. When I am member for South Toronto I am going to continue in Parliament this battle for a showdown. Among those who may be questioned will be the Conservative nominee for West York, who will then be a private gentleman.
I shall ask what protection the Canadian people have at present against combines, trusts and mergers. I'll answer here and now, none whatever.
I would like to ask the hon. gentleman whether with the staff and organization of the Department of Labour, he has undertaken to carry out and wage this battle which, at Mimico on 24th November last, he promised to wage, and if not whether he intends to carry out the promise? If so when and how?

The hon. member's question has nothing whatever to do with the Department of Labour but I will answer by saying that no action has been taken or will be taken through or by the Department of Labour to do the things to which my hon. friend refers; and I here and now suggest that I was rather optimistic in regard to certain things at that time.

I agree with the Minister of Labour that there is no power of compulsion in the department to compel the employers and the employees in the building trades to get together; but if there is no power of compulsion, would it not comport more with the dignity of this country if the minister did not use the language of compulsion? When a minister of the Crown uses the language of compulsion, saying what people " must and shall " do, that signifies that the power of compulsion is behind the language; and when the power of compulsion fails it does not comport very well with the dignity of the country or with the dignity of the office which the minister holds.
The next point I want to make is this: The minister through the campaign painted a lurid picture of what he described as trusts and combines which he designated as the enemies of the people. They were described as foes to be fought, as the oppressors of the real people of the country -the common people of the nation. Does he really think that the man whom he joyfully painted as acting in that role- and he was joined in vigorous language day after day and night after night by the leader of the Progressive party in denunciation of Dominion Textiles and all that pertained to them-does he think that the head and front, the founder, the centre, the heart, and everything practically, of Dominion Textiles is the right representative of Canada at an economic conference? If I believed what the minister expressed before the election, and if I believed what the leader of the Progressive party expressed over and over again, and Sir Charles Gordon were appointed to represent this country at an economic conference- a man who was declared to be the common
Supply-Labour

enemy of the people of Canada

I would feel like getting up in Parliament and saying so. Why is it there is silence on the part of the minister and the Government after Sir Charles Gordon is selected? Why is there silence on the part of the Progressive leader in Parliament after Sir Charles Gordon is selected?	Does not all this
seem very strange?	Certain things, of
course, were brought into the arena of vituperation, hut none so much as Dominion Textiles. That organization was held up as the child and creation of the late Government, and those who controlled it were represented as the dictators of the Government policy, pressing their heels on the neck of the common people, without sentiments of real patriotism for the nation as a whole, and selfish aggrandisers interested only in the accumulation of wealth. Is such a man as Six Charles Gordon a fit representative of the Dominion, and of labour, along with the rest of the Dominion, at any conference at all? How could' hon. gentlemen have been sincere, and then sit silent when such a selection was made?

Two or three hon. gentlemen have referred to Sir Charles Gordon, and to what I said in the campaign. I never mentioned Sir Charles Gordon's name throughout the election, and 1 challenge any hon. gentleman to produce proof to the contrary. Furthermore, I never gave consideration-
Did the hon. gentleman mention the Dominion Textile Company and one of the presidents of it?
One at a time, please. I never thought about Sir Charles Gordon during the campaign. I never dealt, specifically or otherwise, with the Dominion Textiles, but rather with certain other concerns.
Will the hon. minister allow me a question? Did he impale the Dominion Textile Company in the city of Toronto?
I referred in Toronto, and at other places, to certain combines in textiles, cement and various things affecting the interests of the common people of Canada.
Dominion Textiles.
I do not think it. I do not think I ever used the words "Dominion Textiles."
I should like to know if we are discussing the Department of Labour or holding a post mortem?

The hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) has made frequent and characteristic attacks, has misled the members of this House and has referred to the hon. leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Crerar).
Order, order.
I do not think those expressions are quite parliamentary.
If they were parliamentary, those are the expressions I would use.
Withdraw.
I want to say-
I think the hon. gentleman must withdraw that expression, and use some other.

If it is your pleasure and ruling, Mr. Chairman, I will be glad to withdraw, although I have the misfortune to come from a country where men do not usually withdraw their statements once made. I say, in answer to the charge made by the hon. leader of the Opposition, that the hon. leader of the Progressive party has already on the floor of this House, in the debate on .the Address, protested against the appointment of Sir Charles Gordon to the Economic Conference at Genoa.
I am very glad the hon. gentleman rose and made the statement. If he said so, I did not hear him. I am very glad he made the statement. He was consistent in doing it. I am not disputing it at all.

I presumed to send to Nova Scotia a very capable officer of the department in order that he might go on the ground in the mining towns of Cape Breton and ascertain what the actual conditions were.
Further on he said-
I am sorry to say that I must have been too presumptuous in sending a federal employee to that district and in that capacity, because when he got to Halifax he was given to understand, in substance, that he had better mind his own business and get back to Ottawa.

What officer of the department was sent; for what purpose was he sent and from whom did he receive the order to come back to Ottawa? The minister must know this.

In reply to the question of the hon. gentleman from Parry Sound (Mr. Arthurs), I may say that Mr. T. A. Stevenson was the officer of the Labour Department who went East to investigate the entire situation and report to the minister. After being in Halifax a short time-I could not say the time without the file-he was given to understand by an official of the provincial government, as I understand the report, that the provincial government of Nova Scotia was amply sufficient unto itself to deal with the situation in that locality, and that there was not any real necessity for a representative of our department to go further than Halifax to look into the situation.

The hon. gentleman
has stated that some officer of the provincial government of Nova Scotia gave this order to come back to Ottawa. Has this officer sent by his department made a report to the Minister of Labour, and if so is that report available to this House?

Mr. T. A. Stevenson made a report as I recall now. I am speaking from recollection subject to correction. He made a report of each mining town investigated during his stay there, forwarding daily reports, and if they were all collected into one continuous report, I imagine we would find a concrete reference to every mining town he visited, or every situation which he investigated while down there.

That does not answer the last question. Is that report available to the House? Further, who was the officer of the Nova Scotia government who asked this man to come back to Ottawa. I would also ask the hon. gentleman as a favour to lay the report on the Table, so that it would be available to every member of the House, and we could see the conditions that this officer found.
Anything in the Labour Department is available to the hon. gentleman and to this House. I will undertake to bring it to the hon. gentleman and to give to it such publicity as he desires.

That is all we want.
The minister did not answer my other
question as to who was the officer of the Nova Scotia government who asked this man to come back to Ottawa.
I would have to look at the report in order to give the information which my hon. friend wants, and which, I judge, he can get from the report when he receives it.

There are
two matters I should like to clear up on the record with reference to these estimates, and I am sure the minister would be glad to have them cleared up. On page 108, there is an item, "one supplies clerk", for which, last year, there was an appropriation of $1,600, and for which there is no appropriation this year. I understand that, last year, no appointment was made to this office and no salary paid. Can the minister confirm that? From the estimate as it appears now, it would seem to be a reduction in staff and a saving.
It has been found possible to discontinue entirely that position for this fiscal year.

I make the statement that no appointment was made last year and no salary paid, and that consequently no officer can be disposed of. This year the Government is not dispensing with the services of an officer or with a salary, but is simply carrying out the policy of the ex-minister in the late government.

My hon. friend will note that last year there was a salary of $1,600 provided for in the estimates for one supplies clerk. I am told now that, by the usual methods of Civil Service promotion and advancement, that gentleman has gone up to the classification of senior supplies clerk at a salary of $1,680, or an increase of $80 a year.

Last year
no appointment was made and no salary paid. That is all I desire to clear up.
I am told that my hon. friend is perfectly right, and I am thankful for the information because I was not aware of it.

I simply
wish to clear up what appears from the estimates to be dispensing with the services of an officer and the saving of a salary of $1,600. My hon. friend does not wish to create that impression when it is not so. Does the same thing not apply to

the next item, "one audit clerk", for which, in the estimates of last year, a salary of $1,300 was provided, and for which there is no appropriation this year? I understand no appointment was made to the office and no salary paid. If that is so, that is all I desire to clear up.

If the hon. member
will look further up the list, he will find an item, "senior audit clerk", at a salary of $1,500. That is where that classification has gone to and where it is specified in the current estimates.
Last year both these offices were not filled and both salaries were not paid.

Civil Government-Militia and Defence-Salaries and contingencies-$015,577.

I understand that this resolution was called on Monday or Tuesday last and was allowed to stand over owing to my absence. I may say that I have taken the opportunity of going through the various items with some care, and I think I can say that I have some familiarity with the particular items concerned. There does not appear to be very much reduction from the estimates of last year as they were amended by
10 p.m. the committee on that occasion, but I think the reason for that is justifiable. The work consequent upon the conclusion of the war is still being performed to a large extent by three branches of the Department of Militia, notably, the Central Registry Office, the Records Office and the Pay and Allowance Branch. The work these three branches are doing is practically all after-war work, necessitating the employment of a considerable staff. I thought, perhaps, there might be a little greater reduction at the present time than these estimates show, but still I cannot express much surprise at the statement now made. Perhaps I might state that, in addition to the staff which is shown upon page 74 of the Estimates, there is a large temporary staff in that department; 400 of the temporary staff are, I understand, to be let out to-day. When I had the honour of being made Minister of Militia and Defence the temporary staff alone numbered 5,280, and last April, while the estimates were before the House, I remember I was able to say that the staff

had been reduced to 1,200 or thereabouts, and that it would be gradually reduced and finally wiped out within the next year or two. I think myself that a reduction of 400 this year is a fairly good showing. That temporary staff, however, is not paid out of the Militia Department vote at all, but out of the Demobilization or War Claims Vote, as it is now called, which will be found in the Estimates, amounting to some $6,000,000 or $7,000,000. It is purely a war vote. These clerks are doing war work and have always been paid out of the demobilization fund. Their services will expire automatically, I should think, within a year or at most two years, when these temporary officials will of course be all out of the service. I would hardly like to say that the minister has saved the country $600,000 as I saw stated in one newspaper, by reason of dispensing with four hundred clerks on the first of this month. Certainly that amount will not be paid to them this year, but no one expected it would be. Automatically they go out because there is no work for them to do. The Demobilization or War Claims vote will also vanish entirely within a year or two. But on page 74 of the Estimates we find, the permanent staff as it is to-day of the Militia Department. Having gone over that as carefully as I can, I do not think any reasonable objection can be taken to it, and so far as I am concerned, the vote having stood over for my presence in the House, I do not think I have any further criticism to offer on that head.

I notice a Director of Separation Allowances and Assigned Pay. Of course, I know that officer was used very much during the war, but I am wondering as to the necessity of such an officer at the present time.
Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM (Minister of Militia and Defence): Although the war is over that officer's work is going on at the rate of two hundred cases a month.
Are they disputed cases?

Until some time ago
that gentleman was a senior clerk. He has been given that title by the new classification, and his work is the same as before, although he is engaged in the Survey branch.

The positions which

The work that these

Are the salaries of members of the permanent staff in the Records Office paid out of the war appropriations fund, or out of the moneys that are being voted to-night?

Item agreed to.
Civil government-Agriculture-Salaries and contingencies, $775,717.50.

The Prime Minister
stated a few evenings ago that the secretaries employed by ministers of the lata government would be placed in such a position that they would receive, as nearly as possible, their ordinary salaries, less secretarial allowance. My late secretary, Mt. Lynton, was first engaged in the Department of Customs; later he was taken by the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) when he assumed the office of Minister of Agriculture. He served him for two years and was then taken over by me. I am anxious to know what the disposition of the minister is with regard to Mr. Lynton, or what he proposes to do in that connection?

speakeroldname: Hon. W. R. MOTHERWELL (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext: We are endeavouring to locate him, but we have at present no vacancy which is worth as much as the position he held previously, and so far we have not succeeded. That, however, is our aim.

I notice a very considerable increase in the amount for salaries from $567,000 last year to $640,000 this year, contingencies standing at the same amount. The total amount voted for

salaries in the Department of Agriculture has grown from $399,000 in 1913 to $640,000 this year-a very substantial increase. Perhaps the minister could give us some explanation of the increase of $80,000 over the amount voted last year.

The increase of $71,680 is due to three causes. A certain number of temporary clerks have been promoted to the permanent staff and get larger salaries, in accordance with the new salary range. In addition to that, there are some nineteen new positions, accounting for something like half the total increase. There is a reduction, however, under the head of clerical and other assistance from $45,000 to $35,000. My hon. friend may think the salaries very high, but if we have a number of these positions vacant to-day, as we have, it is because the salaries are not sufficiently high to attract applicants to fill the vacancies. The position of Dominion Cerealist, for instance, will be vacant in June. The positions of Dominion Agrostologist and of Plant Pathologist have not been filled yet. Taking them altogether, I do not think that the key men in the department are overpaid. As a matter of fact, we have some difficulty in retaining them at their present salaries.
I should like to ask why $10,000 additional is necessary for travelling expenses. I was under the impression that the cost of travelling was coming down to a certain extent.

There are a number of assemblies and conventions held, some every year, and others at longer intervals, at which the department is represented. The Agricultural Institute meets at Rome this year, and we shall have representatives there. Then there are always a certain number of conferences in connection with live stock and other matters at which we are represented. Some of the travelling expenses that were formerly charged up to the branch vote will this year be charged to this item specifically set aside for travelling expenses. The main increase is due to these overseas conventions being held this year.

A number of new positions are being filled this year, such as Dominion Bacteriologist, Chief of Feed Division, Specialist in Ornamental Horticulture, two Assistant Entomologists, and so forth. It seems to me that agriculture is top heavy at the present time with pro-

S up ply-Agriculture
fessional men. It is too expensive altogether. Was there a call for these new appointments this year?

We have not had a Dominion Bacteriologist in the department hitherto, but if my hon. friend has been reading the newspapers and is acquainted with the legislation passed last session, the Dairy Produce Act, he will know that a great deal of attention is now being paid to the question of bacteria in milk and dairy products generally. Then there is the question of soil bacteria. It has been found as we go along in our agricultural research work that bacteriology plays a far more important part in agriculture than we ever dreamt of some years ago. This man will have to deal more particularly with dairy products and soil bacteriology.
With regard to the Chief of the Feed Division, it is proposed to subject our various feeds to an analysis to guard against any dilution or disease in the seed. It includes bran and shorts, and all kinds of stock feeds.
The specialist in ornamental horticulture will be used at the Dominion Experimental Farm. That farm is a rendezvous for visitors from all over the Dominion, and it was thought that a little more attention might be paid to ornamentation of the lawns, shrubberies, and that kind of thing.
The Assistant Chemist is required because the chemist's work is growing and he is unable to take care of it himself. Many samples of soil are sent in from time to time, and in order that we may intelligently apply artificial manures, it is necessary to analyze different soils to ascertain what manures are best adapted to them.
With regard to the Assistant Entomologist, I am sure we must all have heard at various times of the tremendous loss to our forests as a result of the spruce bud-worm and other insect pests. The department sends out scouts from the Entomological Branch for the purpose of locating these insects and directing the activities of the lumbermen to the affected parts of their limits, so that they can cut down their trees and use them before they are destroyed by these bark beetles and other insects. As a matter of fact, we are going to be short even with these new men.

I am not in any mood to criticise the estimates of the Department of Agriculture, because since my appearance in this House I have been quite convinced that of all departments of the Government the Department of Agriculture has been used the most niggardly in the matter of expenditure. I have made a point of that throughout the country. The minister has mentioned the work done by our Entomological branch and in that connection an incident comes to my mind which happened some years ago at a time when the cut worm was very bad in the West. I mentioned it simply to urge that the Entomological branch has been perhaps in a more or less starving condition so that research work could not be carried out thoroughly, with the result that we who were engaged in agriculture and suffering much loss annually through the depredations of insects would sometimes have to challenge the advice that was given out by the branch. On this occasion, I was driving my team up and down the field, and as the horses were warm I stopped them and walked into an adjoining field of wheat. I had been reading Bulletin No. 32, I think it was, of the Entomological branch, dealing with the cut worm, and according to the advice given in that bulletin all these cut worms should at that time in the morning have been under the surface. It was about eleven in the forenoon and the sun was shining very strong when I walked into my field of wheat and saw, I should judge, a million cut worms in a given space, some going north, some south, some east, some west. I said, "My, according to information in a certain pamphlet you fellows should all be under the ground. What are you doing here?" I wrote to Mr. Criddle about it, and we exchanged several letters, and in the end-I am not saying this boastfully at all-he informed me that my contention was right, that the instructions given in this pamphlet were wrong, and he asked me to continue my research work.
My point is this. The professional man whose money is secure, being voted by this Government, is in a much more favourable position for carrying on research work than the practical man who is concerned with making his living, and consequently I ask that adequate provision be made both in the estimates and in the staff of the Entomological branch so that those who are making their living by agriculture may receive real assistance through entomological research work, which the individual on the farm has not the time to carry on. As I said before I believe that many of the branches of the Department of Agriculture have been starved in the past for the want of funds, and I make this special
Supply-A griculture

plea particularly on behalf of agriculture and of the producers of Canada. I read in the records of last year that the loss to agriculture from insect pests amounts to no less a sum than $120,000,000. A few days ago I put a question with reference to the methods employed by the Government in dealing with insect pests. I asked, for instance, about chlorine gas. I was informed that chlorine gas was considered too expensive to employ in the destruction of insects. That may be true; but the expense of chlorine gas does not prevent its use'in the destruction of human lives. If we entertain a proper conception of the value of the agricultural industry surely we shall not hesitate to employ chlorine gas, or any other remedy, which will enable us to prevent the wholesale losses that result from these insects. Let me point out that the vacant lands held by this Dominion in our western country form veritable breeding grounds for the grasshoppers, cutworms, and many other insects injurious to agriculture, of which I have been complaining. These vacant lands are also breeding grounds for gophers and other pests-menaces to the growth of wheat and other products Of the soil, and in view of this fact the Dominion Government must assume the obligation to combat these pests which live upon the Dominion Government's land. We settlers can take care of our cultivated areas and we do so; but when we have taken the necessary precautions in the shape of spreading poisoned bait we see when we come out the next morning hordes of grasshoppers emerging from the vacant Dominion lands, spreading in all directions, and all our work, onerous as it is, has to be done all over again, to say nothing of the additional expense incurred. I earnestly urge the Government to appropriate sufficient money to wage a determined fight against these insects and other pests which commit such depredations in the west.
I understand that Mr. Duncan Marshall is in the employ of the Department of Agriculture. Which of these positions does this official fill?
He does not belong to the inside service.

Reference has been made to a position which was shortly to become vacant. Am I correct in understanding that this position has ,J)een vacated by Dr. Saunders, who was identified with the research and experimental work which resulted in the origination of

the variety of wheat known as Marquis wheat?

My hon. friend refers, I think, to Dr. Charles Saunders. He and his father were closely identified with the experiments which resulted in the discovery to which my hon. friend refers-both of them worked together.
I am informed that this position has become vacant owing to the resignation of Dr. Saunders on acount of ill health?
Yes.
Is this position being filled; also is any provision being made for Dr. Saunders, or has he made any application for assistance of any kind?

Is it true that another Professor Saunders-in this case in Nova Scotia-has resigned from the Department of Agriculture? The official to whom I refer has been engaged in demonstrating the efficacy of poisons for the potato bugs and other insects.
I understand that what my hon. friend states is the case. The officer was an entomologist.
Why did he resign?
I do not know.

I have understood he resigned because of the inadequacy of his salary. I feel that Professor Saun-der's resignation is a distinct loss to the Dominion, especially to the eastern section of Canada where we grow large quantities of potatoes and encounter serious difficulties with varieties of insects that destroy the crop, to say nothing of rust and other plant diseases which affect potatoes. I repeat that it is a distinct loss to the potato growers of eastern Canada that we should lose the services of Professor Saunders.
My hon. friend's remarks further illustrate the difficulty to which I was referring. I am informed that Professor Saunders resigned because he received a better offer from elsewhere.

Prom the Unitec
States?

Yes, these offers invariably come from the United States. We experience very active competition from that source in regard to qualified scientists. Under the provision as to salary we were not able to meet the competition and we had to let him go.

What salary was
he getting?

I do not know.
That comes under the outside staff. We have not that information here.

Does your plant
pathologist come under this head?

Well, he is under civil government, but we have plant pathologists who will come under the vote for outside staff in connection with the different farms, the information regarding which will be given while we are considering the general estimates of the department. I understand that we have lost pathologists there also for the reasons that I have indicated. We will go into that more extensively when we have the general estimates up.
I hope so.

What are the duties of the chief car inspector?
Supply-A griculture

This gentleman's duties are to inspect the fumigation and cleansing of the stock cars under the provisions of the Animal Contagious Diseases Act. He has charge of the inspectors, who look after fumigation and general cleansing of the stock cars.
Have you inspectors all over the country?

Yes, located at
strategic points all over Canada.

We have provision made
for the Dominion Apiarist, who is an adviser in the keeping of bees. It is not my intention to object to this item, but I wanted to draw the attention of the minister to a circumstance which exists in my own district, the Moose mountain country. Several farmers in that part of the country, owing to the shelter provided by the Moose mountains, attempted to go into the business of keeping bees, and with more or less success. These men have all communicated with me, and asked what assistance might be given them in the way of advice, or what advice the department had to give them, which would be applicable to their particular district. They feel that they should not do all the pioneer work, and I would suggest that perhaps this expenditure might be increased to help out conditions existing in the West. The hon. gentleman is well acquainted with the fact that it is difficult for the people in the West to raise bees. We have small fruits and none of the larger fruits, and the production of honey in that western country would be a wonderful thing, particularly as a weapon to defend ourselves against the encroachments of our British Columbia friends who want to charge us 90 cents extra duty on apples. I think these men who have done much of this bee-keeping work around that country should get a little assistance in the way of advice at least from the department based on information they have received from experiments carried on in a community where conditions are the same as exist in the West. I would ask the minister if any provision is to be made to give advice to farmers as to how it is best to keep bees so that they may produce honey for home consumption.

That is exactly
the object of his appointment. The apiarist is assistant to the Dominion Apiarist. The Dominion Apiarist has charge of the bee work of twenty-two experimental farms, and his assistant is at liberty to travel through the length and breadth of the land for the purposes mentioned by my hon.

friend. This is a work which is neglected. The little tiny bee looks small to the farmer, but the time has come when we must look into small things in connection with agriculture, if we are going to make the best of everything that we can avail ourselves of.

What is the duty of
the fertilizer inspector? This is a new appointment.

The principal
work is to take charge of the experiments in connection with the application of the fertilizers, so that he may be able to report back to the people just what the results are from the use of the fertilizers.
I expect to bring down a consolidation of the present Fertilizer Act, with extensive amendments this year. It is for the purpose of superintendence, and, in addition to that, the carrying out of the act, to see that the fertilizers are of a particular strength in certain important constituent parts. Perhaps that would be the duty of the chemist. This appointment is principally for the purpose of conducting experiments with fertilizers. The officer will first analyze the soil to see what it is deficient in, then apply the fertilizer and report back to those interested.

I am as much interested in fertilizer-because we use it in growing potatoes-as my hon. friends from the West are in wheat. Potatogrowing is the chief industry in New Brunswick. I do not see how you can expect to get an inspector for $1,900. The chief canning inspector gets a salary of $2,660. It looks to me as though the fertilizer expert would command a larger salary than the canning inspector. I am as much in favour of economy as anybody in Canada, because nobody realizes the necessity more than I do, but I think it is false economy to try to employ a specialist at the price of a common day labourer, because you will not get him at that price.

I think you are quite right in that respect. We find it pretty difficult to keep up with our work just now, and with reference to the item I read a few moments ago " New positions and promotions," we expect to promote one of the officials, and put him into a higher grade. He will begin at the bottom salary, and get automatic increases for two or three years, whatever the various steps may be, and this $4,000 will take care of that. I do not know exactly why it was put in at such a low rate. It is a

Supply-Agriculture
new position entirely, and the salary range has not been fixed, we just simply put it in at that figure until such time as we could put it through the Civil Service Commission, with the salary raised and all that sort of thing. It is rather complex and difficult to understand. I have been trying to grasp it for the last three months and I am in my A B C's yet, but I think I understand a little more about it than I did when I began. It is one of the most complicated pieces of machinery I ever saw.

I am not finding
fault with the salary. I do not think you will be able to get a competent man for that salary.

I do not think
so.

And I think my
friends from the West hardly realize the importance of it to us in the East. We use a ton of fertilizer to the acre to produce a crop of potatoes, we pay as high as $100 a ton for the fertilizer, and it sometimes proves very unsatisfactory. I think you will understand the necessity of having a good man as a fertilizer expert. I know a hundred farmers in one locality absolutely refused to pay for the fertilizer two years ago, because it not only did not produce a crop, but it destroyed the soil. They were to pay $100 a ton for it, and they used a ton an acre. Some of the men ploughed it in, and sowed grain in the soil. Others left a few potato plants in the ground and did not get any results. The fertilizer company entered action against one man as a test case to collect the price of the fertilizer and seventy odd farmers combined to fight the case, and put up the money. Yet the fertilizer company has not brought the case to trial, although it is two years old. A sum amounting to $70,000 is involved in the matter between the farmers and the fertilizer company. I hope when the ministers new fertilizer bill comes down, it will cover the case more fully than the old act did. Last year I brought up an amendment to the Fertilizer Act, in an endeavour to remedy this condition. It received its first and second readings; it was referred to the Committee on Agriculture by the then Prime Minister; it was unanimously endorsed by that committee; but notwithstanding that fact and the fact that the committee reported it back to the House at least a month before Parliament prorogued, the government failed to bring my bill up for third reading. I da not know whether the reason was because the representatives of the fertilizer company, who came and fought the bill before the Agriculture Committee, stayed around a week longer lobbying in the House. I noticed that the next day after the Agriculture Committee had reported the bill back, they were going around with long faces. I think the barber must have charged them half a dollar to shave them that morning, their faces were so long. Their faces shortened gradually during that week, and they finally went away with broad smiles. My bill was not brought up for third reading, which is merely a matter of form and takes a very short time in the House, and accordingly it lapsed. When the ministers new fertilizer bill comes down, I hope it will cover the subject very fully. I also hope he will be able to get an expert, through whom the farmers will be able to get some redress in a case like that I have spoken of.

I will promise my hon. friend that the Agriculture Committee will have full opportunity to deal with this bill when it comes down, because it is my intention to refer the bill directly to the committee. I am disposed to think this salary will not get the party desired. I had an explanation from Dr. Grisdale before he was waylaid in Ottawa the other night and was so maltrfeated that he was not able to get around for some time. There was some special reason why he thought at that time he could get a man for the salary; but inasmuch as there is an appropriation to provide for a probable increase, I think we shall be able to meet the situation. We do not want any third-rate man; there is no place in the department or anywhere else for poor men. If you are going to get a good man and if you wish to retain him, you must pay a good salary I forget why this salary was put at $1,920 but there is some provision for the highei rate, if we get the consent of the Civil Service Commission, and I think we shall.

Perhaps it might be appropriate just now to go back to the first part of the session when we had a number of speeches in the debate on the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne. Many congratulations were offered. I am going to congratulate the leader of this Government (Mr. Mackenzie King) on securing such a man as the present Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell). Perhaps



Supply-Agriculture
it is appropriate that I should do so because we lived within a few miles of each other over thirty years ago, and I have known him ever since. I think I may say that, amongst the men that were available at that time to fill this position, I know of no man who commands the respect and confidence of the people of Saskatchewan amongst all classes, not only Liberals, but Progressives and Conservatives, to the same degree as the present Minister of Agriculture.
I was going to ask a simple question. I was quite interested in the remarks about rust. I thought it was significant that the minister connected his remarks about filling the position of plant pathologist and the salary required to get the proper man, with the fact that there were only two or three on the continent who could successfully cope with the question of rust. From the minister's knowledge, what chance does he think there is of successfully coping with the rust question? The losses are enormous, and I was rather of the opinion that, so far, there was no one who could successfully cope with this great evil. I thought, perhaps, from the minister's remarks to-night he had some inkling that they were making some headway and had some chance of finding a remedy.

Before answering my hon. friend's question, I should like to express my appreciation of his very kind remarks with respect to myself. I can remember the time, not so long ago, when my hon. friend was the first secretary of the Territorial Grain Growers' Association, including Saskatchewan and Alberta, and I was the president for the first five years of its existence. I can appreciate my hon. friend's very kind remarks in connection with our relations in those days. I do not exactly know how it has come about that this aisle is between us at the present time, but we shall look forward to the time when, perhaps, the distance between us will be lessened.
The minister is on the wrong side.

Referring more
particularly to the question of rust investigations, I may say that progress has been somewhat slow. I can recall now, over fifty years ago, my first experience of rust in Ontario, more particularly with respect to winter wheat. It was looked upon as a very mysterious visitation; it was thought to be associated with climatic conditions. Certain days were then spoken of as "rusty"

days. Intermittent blinks of sunshine and rain, calm, warm, murky nights and mornings, we knew, were conducive to the development of this parasitic spore. Of later years we came to the conclusion that we knew very little about it, and now our research men are investigating in all directions to find some remedy for it. They seem to think the remedy is along the line of plant resistance, of breeding a wheat plant of sufficient resistance to fight off the attack itself. Just as Dr. Saunders, by plant breeding, discovered a wheat known as "Marquis," somewhat similar to, but very much earlier than the old "Red Fife," so it is thought there may be discovered a wheat plant that will be able to resist the ravages of this rust fungus. I saw in the local papers the other day some American research workers had discovered a smut-resisting wheat, and I am sure some of my hon. friends must have noticed it. Smut has sometimes been referred to as a twin brother or sister of rust, although there is no relation between the two, but it is one of our enemies in the West more particularly. It is thought, if these researches are taken up exhaustively, we shall be able to discover a rust-resisting wheat and other rust-resisting cereal plants. Just the same as animals are resistant ti disease, as has been well established, sc plants are also resistant, some more so than others, to diseases of this nature. I may say to the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, that the progress in that direction has not been very rapid. We have made the discovery, that in the West these invasions usually start down about the Gulf of Mexico in the spring of the year. In another two or three weeks, you will have the wheat planted; in fact, it will be green there now. If they have a severe attack of rust down in Oklahoma and around the gulf, about the beginning or middle of May, and later on in Kansas, it is almost certain that western Canada will have an attack sooner or later. Sometimes, it occurs so late in the season that it does not do very much harm. If it starts sufficiently early down in the south, it has to travel, and travel against the prevailing winds; it comes up through the Dakotas and Minnesota, into part of Saskatchewan, but mainly into Alberta. By the time it gets that far west or northwest the grain is ripe and safe from its ravages. How it travelled had always been a mystery, but experiments made with balloons showed that at an altitude of three or four miles the rust spores travel

Supply-A griculture
in the cross currents going in an opposite direction to the currents at a lower level. Those spores have been found fertile even at that altitude. That will explain in a measure how rust travels so rapidly in a northwesterly direction against the prevailing wind. We know that it does travel, and that it is more or less epidemic. Once it gets started it develops very fast even though the climatic conditions may not be very favourable to it:	but
if the climatic conditions in the south are favourable, it gets to the northern latitude before the harvest is over. Experiments so far have not led to any particular conclusions; we are feeling our way and are getting sufficient foundation material to know in what direction to act, but it will take some years to reach this stage. Up until quite recently we knew very little about this pest. This much, however, has been established, that the barberry bush is the intermediary or host-plant that makes it possible for this fungus growth to develop. Without the barberry it is questionable if it could find another host-plant to serve its purpose. Therefore, wherever we find the barberry bush we would be well advised to look upon it as a noxious weed and destroy it. As a matter of fact some of the western provinces are now treating the barberry bush as a noxious weed.

Is the Department of Agriculture carrying on any work with the object of combating the ravages of the spruce bud moth of eastern Canada? All over the maritime provinces and Quebec the situation is becoming very serious.

I am almost
ashamed to admit that the only way in which we are taking care of that extensive work is by the addition of this one lone entomologist we spoke of a moment ago. That is one of the many requirements that we have to attend to; there is no question about that. When my hon. friend on my left (Mr. Fielding) gets his revenues in a more buoyant condition I will apply to him and may get an appropriation for a good many more entomologists. The ravages of this spruce bud worm are tremendous, and arte measured not in tens of millions of dollars but in hundreds of millions. I was given the information by a gentleman recently, but the figures are so alarming that I hesitate to quote them. This matter comes under the Department of the Interior, but there is a certain amount of interchange of work, and on request from
38i
that department we do a certain amount of scouting for the purpose of discovering where the invasions of this pest are most threatening so the lumbermen may cut the timber before it is quite destroyed. We are not doing much, but we have to cut our coat according to the cloth. I do not think that is a good policy in this case, and I would1 certainly 'like to giet more cloth somehow or other. The next war, it is said, must be against insect life. The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gould) I do not think is unduly alarmed at all, for he comes from a district which by dear experience knows the ravages made by insect pests.
Are the provinces taking up this work themselves?
Yes.
Is the Department of Agriculture co-operating with them?

Yes.
Mr. CALDWjELL: The hon. minister speaks of the loss in dollars, but it cannot be computed in dollars at all. I think we hardly realize what it means to eastern Canada if the spruce bud moth continues its ravages. Unless it can be checked there will be no pulp to make paper and no lumber to build houses. The spruce forests of eastern Canada are different from those of the West, where I have also spent a considerable time. The spruce is a perpetual growth, the trees varying from the size of one's arm up to the largest sizes, all being intermingled, and as the large trees are cut the young growth develop and give a crop of lumber every ten years upon the same ground. But in New Bruswiclc-and I know that province best-it is estimated that 50 per cent of the standing spruce, both large and small, has been killed already by the spruce bud moth, which means that for generations to come this land will be barren, it being generally unfit for agriculture, and simply a lumber preserve. Our spruce forests are what the province of New Brunswick derives its revenue from almost absolutely, and I think the Dominion Government will be well advised to take some steps to explore the possibility of combating this menace. It looks to me to be a big problem. I have seen the air full of these moths fluttering around the tops of our spruce trees, and as a result of their ravages you will notice the buds turn red as if they had been scorched, and the tree dies in one or two years. It is not merely a matter of dollars and cents; the preservation of the future supply of our

The maritime
provinces and Quebec are taking steps to preserve their forests, and a fairly extensive reforestation plan is being carried out in Quebec now. This is such an interesting subject that I may be excused, Mr. Chairman, if I refer to the Main Estimates *-and this will also relieve the anxiety of my hon. friend from Assiniboia-where it will, be found that provision is made for dealing with other insect pests. At page 22 we have an appropriation for the administration and enforcement of the Destructive Insect Pests Act. In the present temper of the country I might be subject to some criticism if this vote was not for such an urgent purpose, as it will be noted that last year the vote was $190,000, as against $235,000 this year, or an increase of $45,-
000.	But that will be found rather small, too, when we come to apply it to the enormous task we are discussing, the fight against these hew insect pests, because, Mr. Chairman, the last four or five years have been so dry not only in the West but also in the East, that a lot of new insect enemies have been developed that we never heard of before. In other words, if you change the climate you change the insect pests. The result is we have to meet the situation with a new vote for that branch which will come up later on.
